rv.q: It's like a greatest hits album on stage.
Modern political junkies and anyone craving a fix of old-time theater thrills should find it hard to resist "Gore Vidal's The Best Man."

Far from being dated, this profoundly cynical play could be the universal blueprint for any political election, especially in Michael Wilson’s classy production toplined by James Earl Jones, John Larroquette, Eric McCormack, Angela Lansbury and other thesps to die for.
What makes 'The Best Man' worth reviving is that it shows us politicians who, however flawed, are also recognizably adult
As fine as Larroquette and McCormack are, there doesn't seem to be any heartfelt anger in their battle — and this sucks out a lot of the play's energy.
Gore Vidal's 1960 political drama about presidential primaries feels remarkably current, though the production at the Theatre doesn't quite capture the play's savage wit.

Unfortunately a thin veneer of currency isn’t sufficient to revitalize a drama that feels positively quaint, despite Mr. Vidal’s winking cynicism about the political arena and his undeniable prescience about future trends in American politicking.
You'll likely applaud much more than that in Wilson's grandly satisfying revival.
The audience might have some of the same delighted feeling at this enormously entertaining revival, which opened Sunday at the Theatre.
This big-star cast worth a wide shelf of past Tony and Emmy Awards deserves a worthwhile play - and they have one.
Thanks to the sterling company here, neither will you.
The play, like a lot of speeches, is witty but long-winded.
So while this might not be the best Best Man -- except for some of the women -- the play still provides enough topical pleasures to warrant blackmailing someone for a ticket.
That both of these great stars are somewhat miscast (and Jones was doing battle with some of his lines at a critics’ preview) mattered little to the demonstrative audience (or to me).
The author's undercurrent of idealism remains as winning today as it did back in 1960 though perhaps even more quaint.
The direction by Michael Wilson makes reality sparkle.
Director Michael Wilson gives each a moment to shine and excitingly paces the play like a thriller.
Nearly every role is cast with thespian royalty

cn.t: Vidal's political drama proves depressingly timeless with its sharp wit, though this starry revival draws mixed reactions. The stellar cast shines, but some critics find the production overly decorous and sluggish, lacking the savage bite the material demands.

vs.sum: The Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, although some side seats may have partial views. The sound quality is generally strong, enhancing the theatrical experience. However, the seating is tight, which can affect comfort, particularly for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is charming with its historic character, and while facilities are adequate, expect some lines at the bar and restrooms.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
